note: The twenty areas, published as text so a mirror gets the content and not just the page furniture.

entries.title: Attention Tunnels
entries.label: Attention Tunnels
entries.plain_language: Your attention goes deep into one thing. The rest of the world fades out. Sometimes that feels good and helps you think. Sometimes it takes you somewhere you did not want to go. Coming back out again is hard.
entries.definition: Entering flow states — or attention tunnels — is a necessary coping strategy for many of us. Flow states are the pinnacle of intrinsic motivation.
entries.what_changes_this: Time that is not interrupted, and a warning before it ends. A tunnel is easy to settle into and hard to get back into once you have been pulled out of it, so the thing an environment can give is a long uninterrupted stretch and notice before the end of it.

entries.title: Penguin Pebbling Cove of Friendship
entries.label: Penguin Pebbling Cove of Friendship
entries.plain_language: Penguins give each other pebbles to show they care. You send someone a small thing you found. A link, a photo, a funny picture. It means: I was thinking about you. It is a way of saying love.
entries.definition: “Penguin pebbling” is a little exchange between two people to show that they care and want to build a meaningful connection.
entries.what_changes_this: Somewhere to put the pebble, and people who know what one is. A link sent with no message is a whole sentence; an environment that reads it as noise is the thing that needs to change.

entries.title: Tendril Theory
entries.label: Tendril Theory
entries.plain_language: When you focus, your mind reaches out like lots of vines. To stop, you have to pull every vine back in. That takes time. Being rushed hurts.
entries.definition: When I’m focused on something, my mind sends out a million tendrils of thought, expands into all of the thoughts & feelings. When I need to switch tasks, I must retract all of the tendrils of my mind. This takes some time.
entries.what_changes_this: Transitions with a runway. The cost is in the retraction, not the task, so the change an environment can make is to stop treating “just switch to this quickly” as a small ask.

entries.title: Mountains of Ruminating Thoughts
entries.label: Mountains of Ruminating Thoughts
entries.plain_language: The same thought goes round and round. You cannot put it down. It gets in the way, and it can leave you tired, cross, or anxious.
entries.definition: When your thoughts are all swirly and you just keep chewing on the same thought over and over and you can’t stop thinking about it and it’s distracting you and sometimes even putting you in a really bad mood or making you irritable.
entries.what_changes_this: Resolution, or permission to stop waiting for it. A great deal of rumination is an unanswered question held open by somebody else — a decision not made, a reply not sent, a rule nobody will state plainly.

entries.title: Cyclones of Unmet Needs
entries.label: Cyclones of Unmet Needs
entries.plain_language: You asked for help and did not get it. The gap between what you need and what you are given keeps growing.
entries.definition: Mismatch between the areas we actually receive support, compared to the areas we would ideally like support.
entries.what_changes_this: Meeting the need. This one is not a metaphor and it does not need reframing — it is a gap between support asked for and support given, and it closes from the side that holds the resources. Advocacy moves that side, and community support holds a person up while it shifts.

entries.title: Rabbit Holes of Research
entries.label: Rabbit Holes of Research
entries.plain_language: You start looking one thing up. Hours later you are still going. You end up knowing a great deal about it.
entries.definition: “Down the rabbit hole” is an English-language idiom or trope which refers to getting deep into something, or ending up somewhere strange.
entries.what_changes_this: Being allowed to go all the way down. Depth is the point, and an environment that rewards only breadth is asking a monotropic person to work against their own grain and calling the result a focus problem.

entries.title: Infodump Canyon
entries.label: Infodump Canyon
entries.plain_language: You tell someone everything about a thing you love. All of the detail. This is a gift, not a lecture. It shows you trust someone and care about them. It can be a sign of friendship.
entries.definition: Talking a lot about a topic in great detail.
entries.what_changes_this: Somewhere it lands as a gift. An infodump is an act of intimacy — it is how a lot of us say I want you to have this — and a room that hears it as domination will get less of everything, not just less talking.

entries.title: Rhizomatic Communities
entries.label: Rhizomatic Communities
entries.plain_language: A rhizome is a root that spreads sideways and puts up new shoots. Lots of small Autistic groups, joined up like that. Some meet online and some meet in person. Nobody is in charge. If one group stops, the rest carry on.
entries.definition: A growing and evolving network of Autistic communities with no hierarchy or dependence on anothers existence.
entries.what_changes_this: No single point of failure. A rhizome survives because nothing at its centre can be captured — which is also why it resists being organised into something legible by an institution.

entries.title: River of Monotropic Flow States
entries.label: River of Monotropic Flow States
entries.plain_language: You are deep in something and time goes soft. It may feel like it has melted away. Your body settles. This is how a monotropic person gets energy back.
entries.definition: Entering flow states — or attention tunnels — is a necessary coping strategy for many of us. Flow states are the pinnacle of intrinsic motivation.
entries.what_changes_this: Let the river run. Flow is how a monotropic bodymind recharges, so time in it is not time off the work — and an environment that treats it as a reward to be earned after the real tasks has the arithmetic backwards.

entries.title: Campsite of Cavendish Spaces
entries.label: Campsite of Cavendish Spaces
entries.plain_language: A place that fits your body and your senses. Somewhere you can work, rest, or be with people without it costing you.
entries.definition: Psychologically and sensory safe spaces suited to zone work, flow states, intermittent collaboration, and collaborative niche construction.
entries.what_changes_this: Cave, campfire, watering hole, library, habitat — and the ability to choose between them. The point is not one perfect room; it is that a person can move to the zone that fits what they are doing right now.

entries.title: Meerkat Mounds
entries.label: Meerkat Mounds
entries.plain_language: You are watching for danger all the time, like a meerkat. You cannot settle into anything, and you cannot find your way into flow. This happens when a place does not feel safe.
entries.definition: Heightened state of vigilance and arousal that involves constantly looking for danger and threat. It is more than hyper-arousal, it is an overwhelmed monotropic person desperately looking for a hook into a monotropic flow-state.
entries.what_changes_this: Removing the threat, not the vigilance. Meerkat mode is an accurate reading of an unsafe room. It stops when the room is safe, and telling somebody to calm down inside it is asking them to stop perceiving correctly.

entries.title: Riverbanks of Monotropic Time
entries.label: River Banks of Monotropic Time
entries.plain_language: Deep focus changes time. An hour can feel like ten minutes. The outside world melts away for a while.
entries.definition: When absorbed in our special interests or passions it can feel like entering a portal. Normal time can feel like it is dissolving, the outside world may feel like it is melting away. This can be really rejuvenating for the sensory system and help to recharge the bodymind.
entries.what_changes_this: Timetables that flex, and people who adapt to needs that fluctuate. Deadlines that arrive without warning, meetings that fragment a day into unusable pieces, and “it only takes five minutes” are all the same request: leave monotropic time and keep working anyway.

entries.title: Shark Infested Waters
entries.label: Shark Infested Waters of Neuronormativity and Behaviourism & Double Empathy Problems
entries.plain_language: The water around everything else. It is the idea that there is one right way to have a mind. It is in schools, jobs and doctors' rooms. You do not just swim in it. You drink it, and it becomes part of you.
entries.definition: The water the whole map sits in: neuronormativity, behaviourism, and the double empathy problem. Neuronormativity is the assumption that there is a correct way to exist in this world. Behaviorism reduces human beings to simple inputs and outputs. The double empathy problem names the mutual incomprehension between people of different dispositional outlooks — mutual, and not the Autistic person’s fault.
entries.what_changes_this: Other water to drink. These are the conditions the rest of the map sits in, made and maintained by institutions, and they do not stay outside a person — the water gets absorbed. Astrida Neimanis’s hydrofeminism is the borrowed frame here (Bodies of Water, 2017): bodies are permeable, and there is no clean edge where the outside stops. So the change is not scrubbing the water out of somebody, which cannot be done. It is that nourishing water has to be within reach — Autistic community, spaces built for the bodies in them, people who do not read you as a deficit. Most of the rest of this map is that water. This is the area with a politics rather than a coping strategy.

entries.title: Beach of Body Doubling
entries.label: Beach of Body Doubling
entries.plain_language: Someone sits nearby while you work. There is no pressure to perform. It is a shared presence, not a check on you. Having them there makes it easier to start.
entries.definition: A “body double” is a person or even pet who is present with us while we work. This provides a gentle form of accountability — their presence serves as a reminder of what we’re supposed to be doing so we’re less likely to get distracted.
entries.what_changes_this: Company without supervision. The difference matters: a body double is a shared presence, not a watcher — being alongside someone steadies the nervous system and carries a gentle accountability at the same time. The moment presence becomes monitoring it stops working and starts costing.

entries.title: Burnout Whirlpools
entries.label: Burnout Whirlpools
entries.plain_language: You have run on empty for too long, without enough left to manage or refill. Now things you used to do are too hard. Rest on its own does not fix it. The demands have to come down.
entries.definition: Autistic burnout is a state of physical and mental fatigue, heightened stress, and diminished capacity to manage life skills, sensory input, and/or social interactions, which comes from years of being severely overtaxed by the strain of trying to live up to demands that are out of sync with our needs.
entries.what_changes_this: Lowering the demands that caused it. Burnout is manufactured by years of mismatch, so it is not cured by neuronormative resilience training, and a return to the same conditions is a return to the whirlpool. The resilience that gets trained into people is compliance under another name, which is why Nick Walker, speaking at the 2026 Autistic Mental Health Conference, put it the other way round: Cultivating resilience becomes an act of defiance.

entries.title: Panic Hills of Low Object Permanence
entries.label: Panic Hills of Low Object Permanence
entries.plain_language: Out of sight, out of mind. Things, jobs and people you cannot see fall outside the attention tunnel. Then you remember, and it comes as a surprise.
entries.definition: Autistic children have difficulties with their understanding of: what’s here, what’s now, what is permanent, and so on.
entries.what_changes_this: Making things visible. Out of sight really is out of mind here — for objects, for tasks, and for people — so open shelving, a visible list, a phone reminder or an app that keeps things in view, and a friend who does not read silence as rejection do more than any reminder to try harder.

entries.title: Forest of Joy, Awe and Wonder
entries.label: Forest of Joy, Awe & Wonder
entries.plain_language: Happiness so big that your body has to move. Flapping, bouncing, dancing. This is stimming, and it is one of the best parts of being Autistic.
entries.definition: Autistic joy is one of our favorite things about being autistic. It can be intense as a meltdown, but filled with overwhelming happiness and excitement. When we experience joy, we feel the excited vibrations throughout our bodies. To release the energy, we do a “happy stim.”
entries.what_changes_this: Room to show it. Autistic joy is loud in the body, and an environment that requires it to be performed quietly is asking for the joy without the person.

entries.title: Lake of Limerence
entries.label: Lake of Limerence
entries.plain_language: You cannot stop thinking about one person. You do not know if they feel the same. The not knowing is what keeps it going.
entries.definition: Limerence is a state of involuntary obsession with another person. The experience of limerence is different from love or lust in that it is based on the uncertainty that the person you desire also desires you.
entries.what_changes_this: Certainty, which is the thing limerence is missing. It is built out of not knowing, and it is a monotropic attention system running its ordinary depth on a person — not a character flaw and not a warning about you.

entries.title: Tides of the Sensory Sea
entries.label: Tides of the Sensory Sea
entries.plain_language: Sound, light, touch, taste and smell come in strong. So do balance, body position, and signals from inside your body. Some days much more than others. It is not a mood. It is your senses.
entries.definition: Neurodivergent people are hypersensitive to mindset and environment due to a greater number of neuronal connections. They have both a higher risk for trauma and a large capacity for sensing safety.
entries.what_changes_this: Control over the inputs, and all eight senses counted. Light you can dim, sound you can leave, fabric you chose — and room for interoception, proprioception and the vestibular sense, which the familiar five leave out. The tide is not a mood, and the lever is in the room rather than in the person.

entries.title: Sudden Storms of Unexpected Events
entries.label: Sudden Storms of Unexpected Events
entries.plain_language: Something changes with no warning. You get pulled out of what you were doing. Your body reacts before you can think.
entries.definition: If an autistic person is pulled out of monotropic flow too quickly, it causes our sensory systems to dysregulate. This in turn triggers us into emotional dysregulation, and we quickly find ourselves in a state ranging from uncomfortable, to grumpy, to angry, or even triggered into a meltdown or a shutdown.
entries.what_changes_this: Warning. Almost all of the damage here is in the suddenness rather than the change, and notice is free to give.
